prompt: Why does a naive extrapolation of the low temperature equation get a hot line backwards?
options: The reaction term saturates at high temperature, so the rate flattens rather than turning, and an extrapolation reads that flat stretch as a rise.
The transport term overtakes the reaction term as the viscosity falls with temperature, so the series combination stops responding to the chemistry at all.
Iron carbonate plates out on the steel above a certain temperature and the layer it forms slows the attack, so the rate turns and falls with further heating.
The fugacity coefficient falls with temperature, so the fugacity the correlation is fed drops away faster than the temperature term can raise the rate.
explanation: The engine handles the turn with a multiplier on the rate. Below a computed onset it is exactly one, and above the onset it falls fast enough to take the rate downward.

prompt: The film multiplier is clamped at one. What does the clamp state?
options: A direction rather than a magnitude, since a film can slow the attack and can never speed it up.
A magnitude rather than a direction, since the clamp fixes how much of the rate the film is allowed to remove on any stream.
The published validity band of the scale expression.
The boundary the engine bisects to find the onset.
explanation: Applying the same expression with no ceiling would let a correction meant to be protective increase a rate instead. Below the onset the engine returns 1.000000000000 and the rate passes through untouched.

prompt: What decides the temperature at which the multiplier leaves one?
options: The total pressure, which is why the onset sits beside the cap flag.
The wetting regime, since a film forms only on a wall the water reaches.
The reaction constants, which fix one onset for every stream.
The carbon dioxide fugacity, from which the engine computes the onset rather than quoting a fixed figure.
explanation: The computed onset is teachable because it is measured out of the engine's own behaviour by bisection and cross checked against a closed form. What the published correlation turns at is a separate question and it is held.

prompt: The course sweeps the onset across seven carbon dioxide fugacities. What do those figures show?
options: It rises as the fugacity rises, from 35.853960 C at 0.050000 bar to 132.297731 C at 60.000000 bar, which is why a high pressure line credits no film.
It falls as the fugacity rises, from 132.297731 C at 0.050000 bar to 35.853960 C at 60.000000 bar.
It holds near 85.058955 C across the whole sweep and moves only when the temperature itself is changed.
It falls to a floor at 35.853960 C and is clamped there, in the same way the fugacity coefficient is clamped above its own cap.

prompt: Across the fugacities the course sweeps, how far does the onset move?
options: Nothing measurable, because the onset is a constant of the scale expression and the sweep is there to demonstrate that it does not move.
10.000000 percent, the engine's own reporting margin.
96.443771 degrees Celsius, which is what retires the idea of a single film onset temperature.
80.984504 degrees Celsius, which is the onset the engine computes at the shipped studio defaults and also the width of the swept band.
explanation: A help guide saying the film appears at a round temperature is wrong at every fugacity except one. The panel prints the computed onset for the conditions set rather than a constant.

prompt: At the shipped studio defaults the carbon dioxide fugacity is 1.344240 bar. What is the onset there, and what is the multiplier?
options: An onset of 80.984504 C, and a multiplier of exactly 1.000000000000 because the stream runs at 60.000000 C.
An onset of 80.984504 C, and a multiplier of 0.206012 because the stream is credited with a partial film at that fugacity.
An onset of 85.058955 C, and a multiplier of exactly one, since the onset at a fugacity near 1.000000 bar is what the shipped case is closest to.
An onset of 60.000000 C, and a multiplier just below one.
explanation: No film credit is taken on that screen at all. Every capstone scenario in this course is deliberately below its own computed onset for the same reason.

prompt: Two of the engine's worked streams sit on opposite sides of their own onsets. What are the two answers?
options: Both have multipliers below one, and the difference between the two is only how far below, which the onset figure records.
One at 119.400000 C with an onset of 79.792274 C has a multiplier of 0.206012, and one at 58.200000 C with an onset of 89.053653 C has a multiplier of exactly one.
One has an onset of 79.792274 C and the other of 89.053653 C, and both credit a film because both onsets sit below the temperature of the shipped case.
One is above its onset and refuses a rate, and the other is below its onset and returns one, which is the refusal the scale door owns.
explanation: The first runs at a fugacity of 1.467680 bar and the second at 0.753085 bar. One expression, two streams, two different answers about whether a film exists at all.

prompt: Hold the composition fixed and walk the temperature up one of the engine's streams. What does the rate column do?
options: It rises without turning across the whole walk, and only the multiplier column turns, which is why the two have to be read together.
It falls throughout the walk, because the film is credited from the first step.
It holds flat until the onset and then falls away.
It rises to 1.508421 mm/yr at 70.000000 C, then turns and falls away, reaching 0.135116 mm/yr at 150.000000 C.
explanation: At 40.000000 C the rate is 1.270135 mm/yr and at 55.000000 C it is 1.401052 mm/yr, both with a multiplier of exactly one. The turn is the film arriving rather than the chemistry slowing.

prompt: On that same walk, at which step is the film first credited and what is the multiplier there?
options: At 70.000000 C, with a multiplier of 0.435371430361, which is the step at which the rate stops rising.
At 100.000000 C, with a multiplier of 0.242520118987, which is the first step at which the rate falls below its value at the start of the walk.
At 85.000000 C, with a multiplier of 0.820838044032.
At 40.000000 C, with a multiplier of 1.000000000000, since a multiplier is credited at every step and only its size changes.
explanation: At 100.000000 C the multiplier is 0.435371430361 and the rate is 0.728051 mm/yr. At 130.000000 C it is 0.141105882050 and the rate is 0.252905 mm/yr.

prompt: Of the six worked streams in this course's source material, how many carry a film multiplier of exactly one?
options: 1 of the 6, which is the shipped studio case, and the other five are all above their own computed onsets.
5 of the 6, so no film credit is in their rates at all.
3 of the 6, which is the split that makes the sweep a fair test of both sides of the onset.
All 6, since every scenario used anywhere in this course is set below its own onset by construction.
explanation: The shipped studio case, which is not one of the six, sits below its onset too, at 60.000000 C with a computed onset of 80.984504 C. Where the multiplier is exactly one, multiplying by it changes nothing at all.

prompt: Where in the chain does this engine apply the film multiplier, and what is the standing of that choice?
options: It multiplies the combined rate after the series combination, and which form the published correlation intends is held.
It multiplies the reaction term before the series combination.
It multiplies the transport term, since a film is a barrier to transport.
It applies the multiplier once to each of the two terms.
explanation: Multiplying the reaction term instead is a different physical claim. The two give materially different answers whenever mass transfer controls, which it does at the studio's own defaults.

prompt: What follows for this course from that unresolved modelling question?
options: The factor is graded only on streams where the reaction term is the smaller of the two, because the two arrangements agree there.
The factor is graded at the Expert tier alone, where a learner is expected to state which arrangement the engine uses before quoting a rate.
The rate is graded and the factor is not, since the factor is a multiplier the learner never has to produce on its own.
Nothing downstream of the film factor is graded anywhere in these three tiers.
explanation: A rate carrying a film credit depends on an unresolved modelling decision as well as on three unsourced constants, so grading one would examine a learner on a question the engine itself declines to settle.

prompt: Every capstone scenario in this course sits below its own computed onset. Why does that clear the arrangement question?
options: The multiplier is then small enough that the difference between the two arrangements falls inside the grading tolerance on every field.
The scale constants drop out of the chain below the onset, so the rate is reached without any held constant at all.
The multiplier is then exactly one, and multiplying by one before the combination or after it gives the same number to the last bit.
The engine refuses to apply the factor below the onset, so a scenario there is graded on a chain the factor never entered.
explanation: It is an identity rather than a tolerance, which is why it is worth stating as the reason. The course asserts it rather than assuming it.

prompt: Which of these is held for literature in the film part of this module?
options: The clamp at one, which is the one part of the correction carrying no source anywhere in this repository and is therefore never graded.
The three constants of the scale expression and the temperature at which the published correlation turns protective.
The computed onset, which is the reason the engine declines to print it and shows only the multiplier beside the rate on the screen.
The direction of the correction, since no source in the repository says whether a film raises or lowers the rate.
explanation: The published turning temperature is a separate question from the onset this engine computes. The clamp itself is arithmetic and it is not held.

prompt: A screening from a hot line reports a reassuringly low rate. What should the reader record beside it?
options: The multiplier, whenever it is below one, so the next reader can see how much of the answer the film credit is carrying.
The reaction term on its own, since that is the figure the rate would have taken had the film not been credited at those conditions.
The published onset temperature for the correlation.
The wall shear, since a film credited by the correlation is only removed when the shear exceeds the erosional velocity limit this module carries.
explanation: A rate that looks low at high temperature is carrying a film credit inside it, and that credit rests on constants nobody here can source. The module holds no erosional velocity criterion at all.
